claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure with inherent microstructural heterogeneity in its as-prepared, unstressed state.
In situ time-of-flight neutron diffraction can provide high-resolution, spatially resolved internal-strain maps of HfNbTiVAl10 during tensile testing.
Strain maps will be collected at 0.1% tensile-strain increments at room temperature.
The measured internal-strain maps can be imposed as dynamic boundary conditions in finite-element simulations.
The spatial distribution of internal strain governs localized yield initiation in the heterostructure.
The spatial distribution of internal strain governs damage evolution in the heterostructure.
Using measured strain fields bypasses the need to assume uniform strain distributions.
Incorporating measured strain fields enables finite-element simulations to account more directly for localized load partitioning.
Direct incorporation of measured strain fields accelerates finite-element simulation convergence.
Strain-map-informed simulations will predict Young's modulus more accurately than simulations using assumed homogeneous boundary conditions.
Strain-map-informed simulations will predict yield strength more accurately than simulations using assumed homogeneous boundary conditions.
Strain-map-informed simulations will improve prediction of fracture behavior relative to simulations using assumed homogeneous boundary conditions.
Predicted Young's modulus and yield strength will be within 5–8% error relative to independent measurements.
Strain-map-informed simulations will run approximately three times faster than traditional full-scale simulations using assumed strain fields.
Traditional finite-element simulations use estimated homogeneous boundary conditions without direct empirical strain mapping.
Insufficient neutron-diffraction spatial or strain resolution could prevent the proposed method from improving predictions.
The hypothesis may fail if measured strain fields do not capture microstructural load partitioning fully.
Behavior outside room temperature may introduce nonlinearities not represented by the proposed model.
